utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Jarcevic, I remind you that you are still bound by the declaration you made yesterday to tell the truth, the whole truth and, nothing else but the truth. Is that okay?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That's quite all right. Place your trust in me to abide by that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Mr. Jarcevic.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: We are going to continue the examination-in-chief. I'll remind you before we start once again that we have to take care to make pauses between my questions and your answers for the benefit of the interpreters. I know it's not always easy, but it would be courteous of us to enable the interpretation service to be able to do its job.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'll do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, Mr. Jarcevic, we stopped off discussing a topic regarding the presence of the regular Croatian troops in Posavina, in the north of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Sava River valley. You explained that there were a lot of problems because the only communication line had been cut off, cutting off the supply route from Serbia and Yugoslavia to Krajina. Is that right? Is that what you told us yesterday?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And I should like to add this fact. The people in Krajina had no electricity.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday you described to us two characteristic cases. You gave us two examples, that 12 babies in Banja Luka and it was the road leading through the corridor, that 12 babies died because supplies didn't come in from Belgrade, equipment for the incubators, oxygen and so on, and the United Nations failed to react and then you described another case to us whereby a man who was in Knin, because the supply route was cut off could not reach Belgrade to be given medical aid. Now, in that connection I should like to ask you the following. Did you contact UNPROFOR? You said you contacted the Security Council but that they didn't react. Now, as the government of Srpska Krajina, did you contact UNPROFOR with your problem?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you, Mr. Milovancevic, perhaps it is in order that I give the name and surname of the man who lost his kidney. He was a famous journalist in Belgrade. He used to live in Knin and his name is Rade Matias. He worked for the very popular Novosti daily of Serbia. Now, when we intervened with the Security Council, this was done both by the government of Yugoslavia and the government of Serbia, and we, from the association of Serbs of Bosnia-Herzegovina as well as many humanitarian organisations, tried to intervene but they were having none of it. The Security Council didn't allow any flights to take place, planes or helicopters and let me remind you that that was because the Serbs were really placed outside the law, outside international law, and within the public -- republics that had separated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I just ask you, Mr. Jarcevic, to please listen to the questions that are put to you and try to answer them as succinctly and with as few words as you possibly can. You've given us a whole paragraph of an answer and you didn't answer the question put to you. The question put to you very simply, and you can answer it by either saying yes or no: Did you as the government of Srpska Krajina, contact UNPROFOR about your problem, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, when the corridor was closed, I was still not in the government of the Republic of Srpska Serbian Krajina at that time, not yet. That is why I explained the other interventions from other circles. Certainly, the government that I hadn't joined yet also intervened via the UNPROFOR officers in Knin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Then your simple answer is, I was no the government of Srpska Krajina at the time. That's the answer to the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much. [Interpretation] Thank you very much, you're quite right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Now, in connection with the combat operations themselves, in the area of Posavina along the border of Bosnia-Herzegovina and Croatia, and those activities usually referred to as Operation Corridor, you said that Mr. Martic was there. Do you happen to know how it came about that the units of the Republic of Srpska Krajina went to the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina to take part in those combat operations?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the normal and natural consequence of what befell the people in the Republic of Srpska Krajina who were under greatest threat at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: According to your information, the information the government had, when you joined it, which was at the end of October 1992, and this operation took place in June and July of 1992, can you tell us what the object of the operation was? Were you able to deduce that? Do you have knowledge about that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The object of the operation was to link up the Republic of Srpska Krajina as a state and the population there, and everybody else, to establish a link with the outside world through Yugoslavia, via Yugoslavia, and that connection could not be established from other sides because you had the Republic of Croatia bordering on that area which had already expelled 400.000 Serbs and many of them had taken refuge in the Republic of Srpska Krajina without the means of livelihood, without any electricity, without the possibility of receiving medical treatment. It was a horrific situation. May I add, Mr. Milovancevic, the following?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, there was no help, not from the international community or from anybody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I think we've completed that topic and we are going to move on to another area. You explained that the situation in the Republic of Srpska Krajina or rather areas under UN protection, that it was very difficult, that there was no electricity, that it was completely isolated, it was under siege and encirclement, do you know whether the Republic of Srpska Krajina received any aid and assistance from Serbia and Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you, it was like this. A lot of humanitarian aid arrived from European countries and other countries as well, through Serbian organisations in those countries and also from humanitarian organisations in those countries. They were organised not to help the Serbs but in by their very nature they were humanitarian organisations and therefore gave assistance. However an impediment or an obstacle to that aid coming in was at the Hungarian border, and as the minister I informed the United Nations of that problem. There were two methods that were applied by the Hungarian customs authorities. They would keep the trucks at the border for a long time which led to two negative repercussions. First of all the food went bad and the medicines went bad and they made it impossible for the people transporting the humanitarian aid to go back to their jobs on time, in Germany, France, or wherever they were living, Holland, or whatever. So this reduced the amount of aid coming in over the ensuing period and then we in Knin lodged a sharp protest against the Republic of -- against Hungary to the European Union the OSCE and so on. And let me just give you another example the Slovenians also prevented aid from coming in to the Serbs and you will become convinced again that the Serbs were really placed outside the law. Two people who were transporting two trucks of -- truck loads of food to Krajina from Switzerland were stopped at the Slovenian/Hungarian border and the officials there tore up their work permits from Switzerland so that these people, the drivers, could no longer return to Switzerland. Now thanks top the fact that the Swiss embassy understood what had happened when we wrote to it from Knin they issued -- these people were issued new pass ports by Yugoslavia and the Swiss embassy gave them new entry visas to be able to enter Switzerland because their families were in Switzerland. So you can imagine the perfidity of those countries and what lengths they went to inflict evil upon the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In addition to the humanitarian aid coming in from the world were there any exchanges of humanitarian aid from Serbia, Yugoslavia, between Krajina and Serbia and vice versa?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Many companies in Serbia helped the Republic of Srpska Krajina and sent in food for people and for cattle, they sent in medicines as well, and I have to say that the government of Serbia as indeed the government of Yugoslavia, they also sent in aid and assistance but most of the assistance that came in to Srpska Krajina came in from Yugoslavia because state relations had been established, trade was functioning, as was economic cooperation, so it was the kind of cooperation that enabled us to survive although we never looked at these figures but the balance of trade was positive, the two-way trade between Yugoslavia and Krajina, Krajina did not have many inhabitants and it wasn't an interesting market for any economy, not even for the Yugoslav economy. But Yugoslavia was a more populated country so everything we produced and manufactured we exported to Yugoslavia. First and foremost, a million tonnes of oil that we had around Mirkovac [phoen], whereas Serbia could not import petrol from other countries because it was under sanction.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you mean to say by that that the economy of the Republic of Srpska Krajina, the branches of the economy that were still functioning exported its products to Serbia and that it was the classical type of trade going on between the two countries?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's quite right and very often when Mr. Martic or the government asked for financial assistance from Yugoslavia, in their letters they didn't say that Yugoslavia owed Krajina everything or had outstanding debts but probably the money that came in as assistance to Krajina was less than the amount owed through exports from Krajina to Yugoslavia. Let me quote an example. We in the government decided to sell oil at 0.80 pfennigs, at what time the German currency at the time whereas that was the world level whereas Yugoslavia received semi-legal shipments from western Europe a neighbouring countries it received oil and had to pay between two and three marks for it, German marks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did the possibility exist, Mr. Jarcevic, for the economy and companies generally that existed in Krajina cooperate with anybody else apart from Serbia and Yugoslavia because of the sanctions that were put in place? That's why I'm asking you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: While I was the minister, we would have visits by Italian businessmen frequently, sometimes from Germany, so these people wanted to do business but after having collected information from their state and police organs they always gave up the idea because they were advised that it was a high risk area, that we were under sanctions just as the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was, and I think after resolution 815 it was and then 871 dating to 1993, unfortunately, and to the shame of the United Nations, if you like, they placed under sanctions the territory which they had previously placed under their own protection that is I'm sure something that will be discussed by politicians and lawyers in the world and who knows which other scholarly institutions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We are now going to move on to another area, the Vance Plan and how it was applied. According to the Vance Plan, troops were deployed, UN troops were deployed on the territory of Yugoslavia, on the territory of Krajina, they were divided into what was known as UNPA zones. UNPAs. Can you tell us what the attitude of the authorities of Srpska Krajina was towards the Vance Plan and towards the implementation of the Vance Plan more particularly?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know under what conditions the Vance Plan was accepted but it was ultimately accepted, agreed upon, yes. Our politician Dr. Milan Babic was opposed to having the Vance Plan adopted and he was against having UN forces deployed in the Republic of Srpska Krajina because he did not expect them to act in a proper fashion, towards both sides, towards the Serb side and the Croat side, but parliament intervened, the president of parliament, Mile Paspalj, was one of the signatories of the Vance Plan, together with Yugoslavia and Croatia, and then the government of the Republic of Srpska Krajina which was quite natural asked that the army be deployed along the border between Krajina and Croatia, because there were intimations in the United Nations that Croatia would violate the agreement and cross over but in New York, the plan was not accepted, they said that the United Nations would be deployed in a very strange fashion according to a strange schematic, as ink spots on paper. Now these ink spots on paper were territories within Srpska Krajina, they were a long way away and set up in those towns.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: For clarity in the transcript, Mr. Jarcevic, you said that the government asked that the army be deployed along the border. Which army did you mean?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The United Nations army, because they were called the protection force. That is, they were supposed to protect the people from Croatia because that's the only axis that the threat wan danger was coming from, because they were to expel 400.000 Serbs from the towns ultimately and let me just add something with your permission. This expulsion and persecution of Serbs from the border was not limited to Srpska Krajina. It was to have been applied to the whole of Croatia but in Krajina, the Serbs were the majority and they organised themselves and were able to prevent in 1991 their expulsion from Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Jarcevic. You have explained that to us. According to the Security Council resolution, were in fact UNPROFOR troops deployed in the form of these ink spots throughout the territory under UN protection; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes and perhaps for this Trial Chamber it is important to know that it was envisaged that with the arrival of the United Nations, the Yugoslav People's Army was supposed to be withdrawn from Krajina. That army was not Serb at the time, as it is presented in the OTP document; rather it consisted of soldiers who were members of all ethnicities and ethnic minorities in Yugoslavia. The commanding staff of the army was -- often times consisted of people who were not Serbs. During the -- for instance, siege of Vukovar, the commander of the army attacking Vukovar was not a Serb, was a Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Under the Vance Plan --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Slow down.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I was asking Mr. Milovancevic to please slow down and to wait for the interpretation before he asks the next question. Remember what you warned the witness about. Warn yourself about it too, Mr. Milovancevic, to wait. Thank you. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. This was to protect me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I appeal to you, Your Honour, to really caution me about speeding because we get carried away sometimes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: According to the provisions of the Vance Plan the heavy weaponry of the Territorial Defence name little tanks, artillery and armoured vehicles were supposed to be placed into depots. Did this really come about? Did the Serb side meet this?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The government of the Republic of Srpska Krajina adopted this and implemented it without any reservations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did the police of the RSK or rather the local police envisaged under the Vance Plan, was it in fact organised in accordance with the plan?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But I said yesterday that Mr. Vance objected with the Minister of the Interior, Mr. Martic, for the fact that many of the police officers were carrying automatic weapons. As I said yesterday, Mr. Martic informed him that this was in accordance with the international standard. Seven per cent of police officers were carried long-barrelled weapons and the needs for that were even higher because Croatia was deploying army on a daily basis and killing Serb civilians in Krajina. He said, I repeat, "Mr. Vance, if the UN army will indeed save our population from further suffering, then we shall give up even carrying pistols."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In view of this answer of yours, I will put the following question to you: The fact that the RSK police had automatic weapons, was it the result of the intention of Mr. Martic and the RSK government to in fact circumvent the Vance Plan?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Regardless of what someone might think about that, they were responsible for protecting the lives of the population, as far as they were able to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know what fell within the competence of the police or specifically was it among the duties of the RSK police to maintain law and order and was this subject discussed by the RSK government?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, the duties of the police do not vary from country to country. However, we have to bear in mind the fact that there was a war on and that the situation was unusual due to the sanctions imposed by the international community. And the lack of willingness on the part of the UN commanders to safeguard our population, as they were in fact obliged to do given that they were called the UN protection forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know based on your participation in the RSK government whether the situation on the ground, and you spoke of these circumstances now, such that it made the job of the police force more difficult, that's to say to maintain law and order?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I will tell you this. I remember that at the time I was the Minister of Foreign Affairs, and that was for about a year and seven months, Croatia had made around 700 police and army incursions into the territory of the RSK. Not a single one of these incursions failed to result in the killing of either police officers, members of the army or civilians, and I'm really amazed at the fact that not a single indictment was issued against a civilian official or a member of the army of Croatia for these crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jarcevic, so far, five large offensives by Croatia against the protected area were mentioned. What in fact are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm speaking of all of these incursions; five of them are just a small sample of these 700.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Let's clarify this. In addition to these five offensives which took place on specific dates, or rather first of all can you tell us which these were?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, I cannot list them all; even those responsible for keeping a record of them wouldn't be able to do that. But let me give you an example.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jarcevic, please, stop there. You didn't understand my question. I asked you to list those five large offensives.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before he does so, Mr. Milovancevic, unless I'm missing something, Mr. Jarcevic said there were around 700 police and army incursions into the territory of the RSK. You talk of five. Where did he mention five? You're talking of, your question was, so far, five large offensives by Croatia against the protected area were mentioned. Mentioned by whom?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with your permission, I will clear this matter up through my questions. As far as I was able to understand what Mr. Jarcevic said, he did not say that there were 700 police officers but that there were 700 attacks on the territory of the RSK during his term of office as minister, with the participation of the police and army, and then my question to him was whether these 700 attacks were in excess to those five large offensives.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, that's precisely what I said. He has testified to 700 attacks. That's what I said. I used the word incursions. Now, you are saying there were large -- five incursions and I'm asking you who has testified about the five incursions? Who has mentioned the five incursions? Because he's talking about 700 incursions and you're talking about five, and you say those five have been mentioned and I'm asking you, before you ask the question to clarify, I'm asking you, mentioned by who?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, yesterday the witness spoke of large offensives. Therefore, I'm distinguishing between individual attacks by police and army forces of a smaller scale and those five large offensives which were large military operations covering vast territories and with the participation of tanks and artillery. I was trying to draw his attention to that distinction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's all I wanted, just to say you mentioned five large offensives yesterday. Can we talk about those? Then you've got all of us with you. Okay. Thank you very much. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jarcevic, yesterday you mentioned five large offensives against the territory under the protection of the UN. Can you please list these five offensives or aggressions?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The first one took place on the 21st of June 1992. That's to say several months before I assumed my duty as a member of the cabinet of the Krajina. I had in my hands a report, and it was deplorable to read there that 40 Serb soldiers were massacred and most of them were thrown into a ravine. On the previous day, UNPROFOR officers had asked the officers in the General Staff of Krajina not to open fire on the border because in the neighbouring town of Sibenik, the international children's day or something of the sort was being celebrated. Of course, our officers did not want to make any incidents. They were a bit relaxed that day, and the Croats actually caught them asleep and massacred them. On the 21st of June, there was this horrific massacre that was committed on the UN protected area but the resolution 762, which was to envisage future steps, contained the following text, that both sides were asked to refrain from further actions and attacks. Something along those lines. Such resolutions always treated equally both the executioner and the victim at the time of such offensives.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt you but do you know whether this offensive was styled in a way, based on the territory where it was carried out?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was carried out on the Miljevac plateau which is the southern part of Serbian Krajina, several kilometres away from the sea side, and from the town where the international children's festival was held.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you briefly list the other large aggressions according to the date?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The next large aggression took place on the 22nd of January 1993 at the time when I was a member of the RSK government. Let me just tell you something I omitted to say yesterday. Based on the suggestion from UNPROFOR, the Croatian and the Krajina commissions were supposed to meet at Obrovac in order to discuss the operation of the power plant but on that day, Croats carried out this attack and luckily, our delegation was not on their way through the area where the Croats attacked. They attacked Ravni Kotari which is the granary and the most crop yielding territory. They also attacked the Perica dam and the area of the Maslenica bridge. According to the information obtained, Croats killed some 700 to 800 civilians, soldiers and police officers. Of course, most of them were civilians. They torched many houses and even damaged a historical monument from the 17th century, that of Stojan Jankovic. At the time, UNPROFOR or UN representatives energetically pleaded with the RSK authorities not to fight back or to respond in equal measure, and that was when the RSK government decided to act as asked and that was when the RSK forces decided not to react.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In order not to go back to this topic again, at the time the Croat-run Maslenica operation was launched, was it not at that time that the Serb weaponry was under double key system, locked up in warehouses?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was when the Serb forces pleaded with the UN to allow them to take their tanks and artillery out of these warehouses, otherwise they were afraid that the Croat forces would reach Knin and God knows what would happen then but even the UN forces themselves insisted that we take the weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did the Security Council condemn this aggression and demand that the Croat forces withdraw?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The Security Council did condemn the action but again, included that statement whereby both sides were to refrain from any armed operations. Since we already had the experience of the Miljevac plateau where the Croat forces were asked to withdraw, but in that case the Croat forces withdrew leaving police forces behind. That was why at this particular point we asked the UN to insist that all the forces be withdrawn, including the members of the army who would be dressed in police uniforms. This however was not heeded. That was something that we constantly insisted on that both the army and the police forces should withdraw from the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember which was the next large offensive by Croat forces against the RSK?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that one we mentioned yesterday, which took place on the 8th of September when Mr. Knut Vollebaek, the deputy of the president of the negotiating conference asked for negotiations over a peace plan. At the time when the peace plan was being discussed, an officer came in to inform them that the Croatian forces had attacked Krajina near Medak pocket which is in the area of Lika.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Am I right in saying that the two large offensives that were to follow were operations flash and storm? Are these the large offensives that we have been discussing?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Your answer was yes. We overlapped a bit.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: My next question has to do with the figure you mentioned, namely 700 incursions by Croatian police and army forces. At the time you were minister. That is to say between October 1992 and April 1994. So these 700 attacks were smaller-scale attacks than these but were nevertheless following a certain rhythm; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Those attacks bore a very specific characteristic. They were part of the information war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you explain to us what you mean by that information war?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was quite simple. The Croats for their part brought in journalists, television crews, and diplomats. And then, from a vantage point, or rather from a point, they attacked our positions and then our forces would respond, would fire back, and all the people that were brought in could hear were shots from our side. And then news was disseminated in the world that it was the Serbs who had violated the cease-fire attacking Croatian territory in such and such a place and on one occasion the Security Council was informed of that by the Russian ambassador Vitaly Churkin and we signed an agreement on the 29th of March 1994 in his office and he was exceptionally prone to implement Croatian policy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jarcevic, the attacks of the Croatian armed forces on territories under UN protection, did the government of Srpska Krajina inform UNPROFOR about that? Did UNPROFOR know about them, about what was happening?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did inform UNPROFOR, the Security Council and even the embassies in Belgrade, and there were two attacks that stand out because the Serb army took prisoner a British citizen and a Dutch citizen as well, in the Croatian army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you wish to say that they were mercenaries over there?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, either that or something else. I can't answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Can you tell us, in addition to everything that was going on, in principle, what was the attitude of the authorities in Srpska Krajina towards UNPROFOR? Was it well intentioned or was it one of hostility, disrespect and belittling them?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The attitude was excellent, perhaps not proper and correct on UNPROFOR's side and this is an interesting point because at one point in time, and if you want to hear me out on this point, about my meeting with an expert for international law brought in from Canada, any way the UNPROFOR men very often didn't want to pay their electricity bills or their rent or their food for that matter because hundreds of soldiers had their meals in our hotels and can you imagine the explanation they gave? They said this is Croatian territory and we shall be responsible for the costs incurred to the Croatian government. We kept writing letters to tell them that that was not the case and that they had to pay us for their expenses and then they said on one occasion that a well known legal expert, MacDonald from Canada, would be arriving to talk to me. A lady called MacDonald. She opened the files and said, "Yes, you cannot demand that UN representatives pay for this because you are not recognised by UN member states." I interrupted her and said, "Madam, China for a time was not a member of the United Nations. Would you be able to run up a debt with China? Or Taiwan, for example? That is an unrecognised state. Could you take your meals in your -- in their hotels without paying them? She was astounded when she heard this, quite taken aback, and then I said that according to the UN charter there are states that are not members, that are states that are not recognised, and those who are recognised. She closed her file, left the premises without saying another word, she didn't apologise, and she just left. However, UNPROFOR continued to disregard the bills it had run up. It still didn't pay and in Topusko when UNPROFOR soldiers sat down to have lunch as they did every day the director of the hotel came out and said there is no food today until you pay your bills. And the money arrived one hour later from Zagreb by helicopter and they paid what they owed and the debts they had run up over several months. So we were very proper towards UNPROFOR. And let me tell you of an incident that took place, when they talked to our people, soldiers from Kenya often told this story later on, these young men were very intelligent young men and I have every respect for them because they concluded something that not even people older people with better education were able to do. They learned a little Serbian and when they were slaves in the 18th and 19th century as the whole of Africa was enslaved by the Europeans, he said, "I'm black. I black, you Serb, it means the same."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you mean to say by that that neither the population or the authorities in the Republic of Srpska Krajina ever had anything against UNPROFOR but quite the contrary that it was in their interest to have UNPROFOR there and to cooperate with them?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. There were no outstanding issues except for these debts and things like that, but that was ironed out too and they began paying for their expenses because they realised that there was no point in them depriving the government of Srpska Krajina with that money because the money could be used to feed the population, care for the ill and sickly and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: That was wartime, was it not, Mr. Jarcevic? You're talking about wartime conditions. You're talking about 700 armed attacks, larger or smaller ones, apart from the five major aggressions and offences in the area of Srpska Krajina. Now, during that period of time did the government of Serbian Krajina ever discuss the fact that non-Serbs -- that any kind of discriminatory measures should be applied to non-Serbs in any way whatsoever?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was like this. The government was strictly bent on protecting those Croats who remained on the territory of Srpska Krajina. There were some enclaves in Lika, a number of villages in Knin, and they were protected and defended but it was a very difficult situation because the people who lived next to them and knew them and had lost some of their family members, some might have been killed in Zadar, Split, Zagreb, so it was difficult to keep people back from the desire to retaliate and take revenge. So I don't want to say that there were not certain crimes that were perpetrated vis-a-vis these remaining Croats or that they were abused but it was never in any organised form conducted by the police, the government, as the opposite side did, the Croatian government organising a pogrom of Serbs in the towns and in the Republic of Srpska Krajina. So that is the difference in attitude and conduct between the government of Krajina and the Croatian government and let me just tell you of one example which you'll find I'm sure unbelievable. You won't believe me. Bull we will have the document I'm sure come up before the Trial Chamber. It is a document of the constitutional court of Croatia dated last year where in a portion of the document, or in one document, a Serbian family from Dalmatia is complaining and the minutes of the government of Croatia is quoted and under one point it states the following and relates to 1990 and 1991, the Serbs are being killed by soldiers, policemen and citizens. Now, something like that never ever happened in the Republic of Srpska Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jarcevic, did you yourself hear about any crimes that are mentioned for instance in the -- this indictment and other indictments, Skabrnja, Nadin, Saborsko, and those place, Kostajnica, Dubica and so on, do you know anything about that? Was there any mention of that at government meetings? Did you receive any reports about any of that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We did discuss it. And I sent a letter to the UN Security Council whereby I wanted to explain the situation attending those crimes. For example, in 1991, for the most part, the clash was between the Croatian separatists, that is to say, the Croatian army, and the Yugoslav People's Army, the JNA, which at the time was not a Serb army, right up until the withdrawal from Krajina it was an all people's Yugoslav army, and Yugoslavia was led by mostly people from Croatia. The Prime Minister was Ante Markovic, a Croat, the foreign minister was Loncar, he was a Croat. The chief of the General Staff was a man who deemed himself a Yugoslav although his mother was a Croat and father a Serb, Veljko Kadijevic. The air force commander was a Croat, General Jurjevic. The army that attacked or rather in the struggle for Vukovar, the commander was a Macedonian. So that army at that time should not be linked to Serb states and Serb leaderships. It was a Yugoslav People's Army at the time and the Yugoslav government was in charge of the entire territory of the former Yugoslavia regardless of whether Slovenia at that time was already considered independent and Croatia considered independent. But as you're asking me about Skabrnja, that was the Yugoslav People's Army over there and in my opinion, those crimes should not be linked to responsibility and accountability of people from the Republic of Srpska Krajina although Yugoslav officers are not to blame as much for those crimes as are the Croatian officers and soldiers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Could I intervene at this stage where you're at this point and he's finished giving an answer? You have said before that the government was bent, strictly bent on protecting those Croats who remained in the Krajina. You recall giving that evidence? Not so long ago.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't understand you. I apologise for not knowing your surname. Nobody told me your surname, Judge, but I didn't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: My apologies are in order. You had said earlier on that the government of the RSK had very, very strict measures in respect of the protection of those Croats who remained in the Krajina. That is what I understood your evidence to be saying a little earlier on, about two questions ago from your counsel, Mr. Milovancevic. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Having recalled that, what were some of the measures that were put in place during the relevant time for protection of Croats within the Krajina, specifically by your government, policy and the measures that you put in place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, for heaven's sake, all -- we considered all the inhabitants of the Republic of Srpska Krajina to be equal. Let me just say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I interrupt you? Can we try to use language that is acceptable in court? I don't think it is necessary to say, "For heaven's sake." It is not an insult but it is just inappropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: You should bear in mind that you did speak of the government being strictly bent on protecting those Croats who remained. That is your evidence so far. I want to thank my learned brother, Judge Moloto, for his observation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you. When I used the expression, "For heaven's sake" it might be milder in the Serbian language than it is in English but I won't repeat it again, no, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now to answer your question. What I said, Madam, is this: That the government of the Republic of Srpska Krajina did not take any steps against the members of any other nation or ethnic group. I don't wish to say that the population did not have some animosity, displayed some animosity towards the Croats living in their midst. I can give the example of Mr. Martic when he was president, that he asked the Court strictly to conduct investigations or rather an investigation over the killing of some Croats and two Hungarians in Baranja, for example. He called for an investigation into those incidents. I don't know the details but the perpetrator was sentenced to a 20 term -- a 20-year term imprisonment, which is a good example of the government taking care that things like that didn't happen. In Sisak, for example, 600 Serbs were killed in 1991. Up until the present day, neither the Croatian government nor international institutions held -- have held anybody accountable, or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: I'm going to have to stop you there. You still have not really got to the meat of what I asked you but our Presiding Judge has reminded me that we need to take our break now. And I'm going to return to that area together with another material area when we resume.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge. I suppose that would be a convenient time to take the break. We will come back at quarter to 11.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, the first thing I'm going to request of you is to advise me how to pronounce your name properly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Jarcevic. Well, you could say that in English it comes from a ram. It means ram.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... what I wish to get from you or rather by virtue of your answer, you have said that, in fact, there were no specific measures in place by the government of RSK other than the fact that there was no discrimination against Croats. That is what I understood. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I didn't really explain everything, the entire security situation. Given the situation in which the population in Krajina were, had this happened in a different country and to a different people, it would probably have been much worse, both for the majority people and the minority people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Very well. We will leave that there. Now, there is another area that has been on my mind. Everything in the case is on my mind but this has from time to time come to the forefront and certainly during your evidence. Now, you refer to the Yugoslavian army, the army of Yugoslavia. Was there an army of the RSK?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you have 1991 in mind, at that time the RSK was only in the making.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Whilst the RSK was in existence, up to 1995, for example, did you have an army of the RSK at any time from the inception of RSK? And I take it you know what I mean by RSK.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the 19th of November 1991, the Republic of the Serbian Krajina was declared and it had its army throughout its existence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Now, you are speaking of the Yugoslav army during the course of your evidence. To which territories does that Yugoslav army relate? And is it distinguishable from the RSK army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The army of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was deployed throughout the territory of the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia in 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Please stop. Which territories comprise the Yugoslavian army and the Yugoslavia that you are referring to? That's what I wanted to get from you, as distinct from the Serbian -- sorry, as distinct from the RSK army.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Based on Security Council resolutions, or, rather, based on a Security Council resolution pursuant to which Yugoslav laws were applied on the UN protected areas the resolution also envisaged the time at which the JNA was to withdraw from the area. There is exhaustive documentation to that effect and correspondence between the -- the JNA General Staff and UNPROFOR. I believe that the last JNA units withdrew from the eastern part of the Republic of Serbian Krajina and if I'm not mistaken it was in September of 1992 and this was something that UNPROFOR officers agreed with and were kept abreast of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Mr. Jarcevic, I'm going to try to express myself with a little bit more clarity because I'm clearly not communicating the evidence, the nature of the evidence that is needed from you which I greatly regret. Now, do you accept that there was a Croatian army? Can we have that question on the record from you? Yes or no? Within the relevant time frame that I have given you. From the inception of the RSK and I have taken it to 1995. During that time frame, was there a Croatian army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Let me take you to the next question. During that time frame, you accept that there was an army of the RSK?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: I'm referred by my learned Presiding Judge that I have been set down on the record as Judge Moloto. I'm very, very flattered but I go on to the next question. Now, when you speak of the Yugoslav army, to which territories or which territories would that army have been acting on behalf of? Bearing in mind that there is a Croatian army and an army of the RSK.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam, I do wish to answer your question. The army of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was present on the territory of the RSK in agreement with UNPROFOR. UNPROFOR and the Yugoslav army had agreed on the dynamics of its withdrawal from the RSK and this was something the RSK government at Knin could have no influence over.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Jarcevic, I do not want history. What I need from you simply is the components of the army in terms of the countries or the republics it represented, bearing in mind that your evidence is on more than one occasion that there was a Croatian army and that there was an army of the RSK. So I'm asking you to state precisely which territories that Yugoslav army represented or would have consisted of. I did not believe that I had such a disability in communication.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam, I don't understand you at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Was the Yugoslavian army representing Croatia at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Again, I'm at a loss. The Croatian army was an army that was formed in an anti-constitutional way because Croatia had seceded from Yugoslavia in an anti-constitutional way. It had formed its army, which it had been arming even before Croatia proclaimed its independence and the army supplies came from European countries. Croatia failed to place this issue for discussion before either the UN Security Council or any other international organisations, and in fact you have this on record. The international community did nothing about the fact that Croatia had been arming itself with the help of Hungary and forming its paramilitary formations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: I don't think I can try any harder. And for the time being, I'm going to leave it there. I do not know if my president, my Presiding Judge, or my learned brother Judge Hoepfel, or learned counsel sell Mr. Milovancevic can take the witness where I need to go, to get an understanding as I would wish it. Thank you very much, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I guess my sister wants me to try and follow up what she's been trying to get out of you. Now, Mr. Jarcevic, please don't refer to UNPROFOR, don't refer to a United Nations resolution, just answer my question. And I think this is what my learned sister wants to find out from you. When you talk of the JNA, that is the Yugoslav army, that is an army, according to you, representing which republics and provinces of the Yugoslav -- of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, you didn't specify the time frame you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The same time frame that Judge Nosworthy referred to.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we are discussing the years 1990 and 1991, the Yugoslav People's Army was in their barracks in all the Yugoslav republics. It was there that the JNA was attacked, which according to UN documentation amounted to an aggression. It was attacked by paramilitary formations of both Slovenia and Croatia. Later on, also by the paramilitary formations of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Jarcevic, I asked you to please not refer to the United Nations or to resolutions. I'm asking you from the point of view of the Yugoslav federal state, not from the point of view of the United Nations, from the point of view of the view of the Yugoslav federal state and from your point of view as a minister in the RSK, what territories did the Yugoslav army represent or have jurisdiction over?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Yugoslav army, as I put it, and I stand by that, was present in all the republics. It withdrew from different republics at different times. From the territory of Slovenia, from the territory of Croatia, from the territory of the RSK and at a given point from the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. It was withdrawing to those areas which were later become the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. Or that's to say Serbia and Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In order to clarify matters fully, Mr. Jarcevic, the JNA was the army of the federal state of Yugoslavia in 1990 and in 1991, which was called the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia. We will call it Yugoslavia for short. In 1990 and 1991, in Yugoslavia, did any republics have their own --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: It seemed to me that counsel was starting to give the answer to the question rather than asking another question of the witness. That's why I've risen to object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Whiting. You hear that, Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I will rephrase the question. So as not to e pose myself to the risk of having my question misunderstood. By your leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's not a question of being misunderstood. The objection is that you are asking a leading question. Don't put words into the mouth of -- into the mouth of the witness. Let me speak and finish. Ask a question so that we get the answer from the witness, not you suggesting the answer to the witness. This is your witness. You may not do that with him. You can do that in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jarcevic, was the Yugoslav People's Army a federal armed force?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, under the constitution it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In addition to the JNA, were the republics able to have or allowed to have their own armies?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they were not allowed to have that but they were able to have the Territorial Defence which had also been envisaged under the constitution but it was merely an auxiliary force in addition to the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Under the Yugoslav constitution, were the federal armed forces in fact a single force consisting of, on the one hand, the JNA, and, on the other, the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's precisely what I wanted to explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us go back to the issue of the Vance Plan and its implementation. It envisaged the return of displaced persons. You mentioned this yesterday, Mr. Jarcevic. Did the RSK, the RSK government, and specifically Mr. Martic, as the Minister of the Interior, and later on as the president of the RSK, prevent the Croat population from returning there because of hatred or any other reason?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We never acted that way, either the RSK government or Mr. Martic. At the same time, we were insisting on the fact that expelled Serbs had to be allowed to return.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Does this mean that you merely sought reciprocity, that's to say that the Croat and Serb populations, which were displaced, had to be treated equally?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But one has to say that there were more displaced Serbs than Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You spoke of five major offensives. You also said that the Security Council issued resolutions condemning these offensives. The Republic of Croatia, as a state which became a member of the United Nations, did it ever incur any consequences or repercussions for the crimes that were committed?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never. It was the only country ever to attack an area that was under UN protection.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday you said that the inhabitants of the Republic of Srpska Krajina after those operations were forced to leave Croatia and that this amounted to hundreds of thousands of people leaving. Did that population, 11 years on, after being expulsed, can it return to the territory of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It does not have any normal conditions for returning, and I would like now to repeat that Croatia is the only country after World War II to place a whole nation outside the law, to outlaw a whole nation, because all the immovables and property of Serb families were confiscated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jarcevic, three days ago, the 150th anniversary was celebrated of the birth of Nikola Tesla, world renowned scientist, he's a Serb from the village of Smiljane near Gospic. In Gospic three days ago the president of the Republic of Serbia went there to celebrate this event and met with Croatian president Stipe Mesic, and the president of Serbia was astounded, and this was carried by the media, that thousands of Serbian villages in Croatia still do not have any electricity 11 years after the war. Is that true? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm going to object on two grounds: One, it's a patently leading question and secondly I don't see the relevance of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What's the relevance of the statement, Mr. Milovancevic, and why do you put a leading question to your witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was not my intention to ask a leading question, Your Honour. As to relevance, relevance is linked to the allegations in the indictment raised by this Prosecution because of Operation Storm, against three accused, in which it speaks of systematic efforts on the part of the Croatian state to expel and prevent the return of the population. Now, I am interested in knowing whether Mr. Jarcevic, as somebody who is always kept abreast of the situation, whether he knows that today, 11 years after the war has been over that electricity or rather the Croatian authorities have not turned on electricity to the Serbian villages makes normal life impossible. So in the 21st century people are living in the dark without electricity because the Croatian authorities haven't seen fit to switch it on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The evidence so far is that the Serbian people have been refused to return. So why would we turn on the electricity in houses which are empty? The ruling is that the question is irrelevant and it's disallowed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. The Defence has no more questions for this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Whiting?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. My name is Alex Whiting and, as you've probably guessed, I'm one of the prosecutors in this case.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning. I did not know that you were the prosecutor. I'm happy to meet you and I hope we'll get on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Me too. One way that we will certainly -- that will certainly assist in us getting on is if you focus carefully on the questions that I put to you and answer them as specifically and briefly as possible. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fully.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, yesterday you testified, it's at page 64 of the transcript, that Mr. Martic, "never expression the hatred towards any ethnic or religious group and those were my own personal standpoints as well. So we got on really well." Do you remember that testimony yesterday?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Completely, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So you -- you and Mr. Martic had similar views at the time; is that right? At the time that you were the Minister of Foreign Affairs of the RSK?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And we hold similar views today, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: But in fact, while you were foreign Minister of the RSK, you on several occasions used very extreme language when talking about Croats and Muslims, isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only when that referred to the states of the Muslims and the Croats and they were brutal towards the Serbian population and I state that today as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, let's look at some of those statements, if we could.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And I'd ask that the -- we look at 02150847, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, while this is coming up, I'll tell you that what you're going to see here is a letter that was written by you and read out to the assembly session of the Republika Srpska on the 11th of September 1993. You wrote it to Aleksa. Buha you're shaking --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know about that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Excuse me. Our screens are frozen. So you're calling something on the screen?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. My screen has frozen as well. Yes. My computer is frozen. I don't have an image on it either.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: For some reason there is a B/C/S on both, of the English and the B/C/S. Your Honour, may I proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may proceed, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Jarcevic, do you see this letter and do you recognise it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. It's mine. No problem there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You wrote these words?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wrote each and every single word.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Let's look at the -- I'd like to look at the bottom of page 1 in the English, and please go to page 2 in the B/C/S. I'm not going to read the whole letter but I'll read one particular passage and it's about halfway down on the B/C/S, if we could scroll down, keep going, keep going, it's about there. And the English it starts at the bottom and it says, "Croatia it" and you wrote this letter while you were foreign minister; is that right? Foreign Minister of the RSK?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And you wrote the letter to be read out at the assembly of the Republika Srpska in Bosnia-Herzegovina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And in fact it was read out at that assembly, wasn't it, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And now let's look at what you say here in your letter. "Croatia is waiting for the Serbs in Republika Srpska to either kill each other off or that they become preoccupied with themselves so it, Croatia, could fill the pits with Serbian women, children, and the elderly. We must not make the same mistake today as we did so many times before. Serbian knights must be on Serbian borders. The villain who," it says "thought," but I believe it's supposed to be "taught," "from his childhood to exterminate Serbian people must not step on Serbian land. Too much of our land was taken away from us during this century for us to be able to give up even one inch of it now." In that little passage that I've read, the villain that you're talking about, taught from childhood to exterminate the Serbian people, that's the Croatian people - isn't it? - that you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I'm saying is that through the textbooks at school, a lot was put out which caused hatred towards the Serbs, led to hatred towards the Serbs and that is true and I have written two or three books in the past few years about that and I have no need to retract a single sentence from the text you just read out. And I can explain the situation to you what it was like at that point in time and I'm sure the Trial Chamber does not know about it, and with the Court's permission, I should like to explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like you to just please to focus us on answering my questions. And I don't think that you have answered my question. The villain that you're speaking about here is the Croatian people, because they are the ones you say have been taught from childhood through the textbooks that you talk about to exterminate Serbs, so the villain is the Croatian people, isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Croatian state, sir. That's what I said a moment ago when you asked me. The Croatian state committed evil deeds against the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm not asking you who --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, please listen to my question. Are you telling us that the Croatian state and the Croatian people had different textbooks?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There would not have been the evil that there was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You haven't answered my question. My question is: Did the Croatian state and the Croatian people have the same textbooks?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Croatian state put out these textbooks to its inhabitants. Ante Starcevic, a racist, is called in these textbooks the father of the Croatian state and he said that the Serbs should be exterminated, the Serb cattle should be exterminated.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And what you're saying here so we are very clear is that the Croatian people have been taught through these textbooks from their childhood to exterminate Serbs. Isn't that what you're saying in this passage?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I was quite clear. The father of the Croatian state, in the Croatian textbooks, used in primary and elementary schools, says what he said and that is that the Serbs should be exterminated. And if you read what the father of the Croatian state said, he said that the breed should be exterminated.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir are you -- aren't you trying -- in this passage, sir, aren't you -- aren't you trying to make the Serb people afraid of the Croatian people? Isn't that what you're trying to do in this passage?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are afraid of the Croatian state. I didn't say that they were afraid of the Croatian people. But I said that the state prepared the population for evil, and it perpetrated that evil several times during the 20th century.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And if you're saying that the state prepared the population for evil, then isn't that the same as saying that the Serb people should be afraid of the Croatian people? Isn't that really what you're saying, sir?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, the Croatian people were not afraid. They believed that the events would not be repeated of World War II. Unfortunately they did repeat themselves and textbooks wield great influence both on the individual and the collective. You can't say they don't. And take up one of the Croatian textbooks and you will see that it says there that the Serb breed should be exterminated, and I'm very happy that --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm going to have to interrupt you because I'm afraid you haven't answered my question. I'm going to put the question to you again: If you're saying that the state prepared the population for evil, then isn't that the same as saying that the Serb people should be afraid of the Croatian people? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I repeat, the Croatian state, and I'm not going to answer your question in a different way. I know that there are among the Croatian people good individuals as there are among the Serbian people. There are good people and bad people on both sides. But then when the state and the church leads the population in a certain direction, then that's what you get.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And, sir, isn't it -- every time you mention what happened in World War II, both at the time and in court here today, aren't you trying to do the same thing, make the Serb people afraid of the Croat people? Aren't you trying to spread fear? Isn't that what you're trying to do, sir?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My dear sir, would your people not be afraid of concentration camps, death camps in Croatia apart from Germany was the only country to have concentration death camps against Serbs, Romany and gypsies and Jews. And you can't challenge that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm going to take your answer that -- take it that you're told us in fact that you were in fact trying to make them afraid. You were trying to make the Serb people afraid and you're continuing that today. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecutor is presenting his views and positions as being the alleged statement of the witness. The witness answered. Now, whether the Prosecution is satisfied with that answer or not is up to the Prosecutor. But he cannot comment on the answer and then deduce a meaning that the witness did not state. He can carry on with his cross-examination, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't think that the witness did answer the question and if he did, he did it in that rhetorical fashion. So I was simply trying to restate it. And I did at the end ask, isn't that right? So I'm giving the witness an opportunity to agree or disagree with the way I've restated the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You hear that, Mr. Milovancevic? The witness is being asked to comment on the answer as it's understood because he had given no answer to the question put to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if the Prosecutor expects a comment from the witness, he must ask him but he must not make the comment himself as being a comment made by the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't understand what you're saying. I understand that this is a cross-examination. This is not a leading. I'm not quite sure what you're saying. And under cross-examination, I can -- it's perfectly legitimate for the cross-examiner to put propositions to the witness and ask for the witness to comment. This is what I've been encouraging you to do when you're cross-examining witnesses so I'm not quite sure I understand what you're saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, yes, I agree with what you've just said. I'm thinking along the same lines, but I objected because after hearing the witness's answer, he took the sense and meaning of that answer and rephrased it and said, "So I conclude that you said such and such."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Because the witness instead of answering the question asked a question. Now, it is not for the witness to ask questions in this Court or in any court. It's for the witness to answer questions so if he asks a rhetorical question, the examiner is trying to put meaning to the question that the rhetorical question and invite the witness to say, is it how I understand you correctly? Is the way I understand you the correct way? Is that what you wanted to say? It's up to the witness to say, No, you misunderstand me, and then explain what he meant. You understand?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That's what I am talking about as well, Your Honour, Judge Moloto, but the Prosecutor didn't ask whether the witness agreed with what his conclusions were. That's why I objected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Of course he asked. He actually said to you in answer to your objection, I actually said at the end; is that right? And it was for the witness to say, Yes, that's right or No, that's wrong. And it's there on the record. If you want to see it, let me go back to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: May I proceed, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may proceed. .

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Objection overruled

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Jarcevic, I'm going to put it to you one last time. In fact, when you invoke World War II and what happened in World War II, when you did so at the time and when you do so in court here today, you're trying to make the Serb people afraid of the Croatian people. Isn't that right, sir? And if you could give me a direct answer to my question, I would be most grateful.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't want to accuse the whole of the Croatian people. By your question you're asking me to do that. I wasn't do that but I am accusing the Croatian state and blaming it because it has the textbooks which can lead to evil. That is what I say in my text.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And the language that is in this letter was quite common in the official Serb media at the time, that is in 1991, 1992, 1993; isn't that right? These kind of words could be found in the official Serb media at that time?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, you can find language like that in scientific works, in historical works, that throw light on the period of Serbian persecution and the killing of Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I didn't ask you about scientific works or historical works, sir. I asked you about the official Serb media so if you could please focus on my question and answer my question. This kind of language was quite common in the official Serb media in the years that I mentioned, 1991, 1992, 1993; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but if I may be allowed to add something, it wasn't even as remotely poisonous a language as it was to be found on the Croat and Muslim sides, and I can give you several examples.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Maybe Mr. Milovancevic will ask you for that but at the moment I'm going to ask you some other questions. You told us that you were the foreign minister when you made this statement. So you made this statement at a time when you say that you were trying to negotiate peace with the -- with Croatia; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, could this document be admitted into evidence, please and given a number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be Exhibit number 861, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, I want to talk to you, ask some questions about your approach to the negotiations that you testified about on direct examination. In your testimony, you went through a series of negotiations that occurred with the Croats. Now, from -- let me ask you this question from the start. Isn't it a fact that a major impediment in all of the negotiations that occurred before you became foreign minister and after you were foreign minister, was that you and the other Serb leaders would not accept a solution that gave the Serbs autonomy in the RSK because you insisted, again and again, on having your own state in the RSK, that the RSK be a separate nation. Wasn't that a major impediment throughout for a peace settlement?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: No because it wasn't an impediment or no, because that was not the aim of the Serb leaders in the RSK?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The aim of the leaders of the Republic of Serbian Krajina was to achieve autonomy in Croatia but the Croatian side never agreed to that. Had it agreed to that there would not have been a war F you remember, the Serbs were asking for full autonomy, cultural autonomy, interpreter's correction, but they weren't able to obtain that either.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Are you telling us that when you were foreign minister, after 1992, that you and the other leaders of the RSK would have settled for autonomy and not a separate state? Do you understand the distinction that I'm making?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Autonomy represents the statehood of the people who are autonomous. This was taken away from us in 1990 with the amendment to the constitution and the Croats never agreed to give us back our sovereignty the way we had it in Yugoslavia. That was the major impediment.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you because I want to try to see if we can make a -- be cheer about our terms. When I say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
