utterances.text: Mr. Whiting, before you proceed, at line -- page 44, line 19, there is -- I am understanding that the Serbs were asking for cultural autonomy, because after full autonomy it says interpreter's correction. Could we get an understanding there? I'm a little bit uncertain. My understanding of interpreter's correction is that he really said cultural autonomy.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter notes that the witness said "cultural autonomy."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Jarcevic, I want to make a distinction between autonomy and separate statehood. Autonomy being rights for the Serbs in the territory of the RSK but the territory of the RSK remaining within the state of Croatia and separate statehood meaning that the RSK would become a separate state from Croatia. Now that I've explained that distinction, isn't it correct that a major impediment to any peace with Croatia was that the -- you and the other Serb leaders of the RSK always insisted on separate statehood and would not accept any form of autonomy? Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting, our point of departure was always to put forth the -- what were our maximum demands because that was the way each of the sides approached negotiations. The Croats would not agree to that. I explained this when I talked about the negotiations that took place at Knin, at Oslo, and London.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And your side, the Serb side, would never accept autonomy, would never accept anything short of statehood; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're not right, sir. This is why. I told you that Redman and Churkin insisted that we sign the Erdut agreement whereupon the Croatian state would become an integral state, but there would be two parts of the state along the ethnic lines but the president of Croatia refused that. Of course, do you know what clout Russia and America had in those international terms? They were the ones offering guarantees for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: We'll look at the Erdut agreement a little later and I think we'll see it doesn't say anything like what you've just described. But let's move on. I want to look at document 02108173. And on the B/C/S -- yes, thank you, perfect. That's exactly the article that I wanted to blow up on, that one right there. Mr. Jarcevic, do you see this article? It's from the 14th and 15th of January 1993, and it's head lined reaction of Slobodan Jarcevic, Minister of foreign affairs. I just want to look at a few passages from this article. First of all at the beginning it says, "I hope the world will realise that all the evil that has come upon the former Yugoslavia comes from Croatia and the artificial Muslim creation, which both initiated the war in an attempt to destroy the Serbian people." Did you say those words, sir?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And I stand by them today. You see the extent to which I was proved right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Really? Well, what do you mean by --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What do you mean by "the artificial Muslim creation"? What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting, thank you for asking me this. The Muslim population is Serb population converted to Islam under the coercion of the large Turkish empire. The Austro-Hungarian empire, Austria and later on Germany, exerted their influence through school textbooks although you seem to claim that they do not have any impact on the young generations. And that was how they became a separate entity to that of the Serb people and that's why I call them an artificial state because they created their state on what was Serb land for centuries. You say that I should not go back to history but history explains everything because the large powers wielded their influence in different ways on the Balkans than they did in their colonial -- in their colonies in Africa. So the colonial powers approached this particular area in a different way. Well, if I may go on, you can see what I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'd like to go on, on the article. A little further down, and I hope you can see it on the B/C/S version, I can't say exactly where it is, but you say, it says, Jarcevic reiterated the view that a monster state, which once already existed, was again being created in the territory of the former Bosnia-Herzegovina. "Monster state"? What is that a reference to, please?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting, thank you for asking me that. I will repeat that as I stand by that today. Bosnia-Herzegovina, as it is envisaged, cannot operate, and that's why it is a monster state. Let me tell you why. This is the kind of country that cannot have common school textbooks, one flag, one anthem. It has to use different terms to those in the Serbian language, and they use Serbian language. You can see that Croats in Bosnia erected a monument for which the Muslims said that it was a monument erected for criminals. So what is going to be the case with their school textbooks? In Muslim textbooks, Serbs are going to be called criminals and in Serb textbooks, Muslims are going to be called criminals. That's why I stand by what I said. I'm Bosnia-born and therefore I'm more than familiar with the circumstances in that country.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm going to keep asking you questions but we'll save a little bit of time I think if you don't thank me for every question I ask you. It will just save a little bit of time. A little further down, it says, and I think it's quoting you here, "Judging by all, a form of federation or confederation with Croatia is being envisaged for RSK, which is unacceptable for us." And then you say, it says, "He" referring to you, I believe, "insists that RS, Republika Srpska, and the RSK, must have their statehood. It is impossible not to give the Serbian people the right to self-determination, Jarcevic stressed." So this is an example is it not, of you insisting at the time as foreign Minister of the RSK that the RSK must be a separate state, that a federation or confederation or any other arrangement with Croatia would be unacceptable. Wasn't that your position at the time?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I still hold that opinion today. I was unable to get around what was decided upon when I was three years old, under 29th and the 30th of September 1941 at the congress in Zagreb --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir you've answered the question. Why is the Minister of Foreign Affairs for the RSK, why, sir, are you talking about insisting on statehood for the RS, the Republika Srpska, in Bosnia-Herzegovina? Why was that an interest of yours?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was the state we had the most close -- the closest relations with. I said yesterday 64 per cent of the land belonged to the Serbs, based on what could be found in land registry offices, and the -- this had had to be taken into account by the other two ethnic groups, especially by private owners, because as you know private property is sacrosanct in the world.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, could this document be admitted into evidence and given a number, please is it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be Exhibit number 862, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Jarcevic, you testified yesterday, it's at page 41 of the transcript, that the government, referring to the government of the RSK, "did not reject a single proposal made by international mediators. We accepted all their proposals and negotiated with Croats." You remember that testimony from yesterday?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That testimony is not true, is it, sir? In fact, you did not accept proposals that would have given the Serbs autonomy in the RSK because you were insisting all along on statehood, isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were the maximum demands on our part. I said that a moment ago and I stand by that still. Even if we were to sit at a table to negotiate with the Croats today, this would be our starting point because we had our statehood before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, it would be your starting point and your end point, isn't that right? You never retreated from that position, isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, how could we have retreated from that position when 400.000 people had been expelled from Croatian towns? How can one place trust in such a country? Would you yourself agree to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So the truth is you never did retreat from that position. You insisted always on statehood and that was the impediment to a peace, isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I repeat: In 1945, we had our statehood, and that's no news, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If we could look, please, at document 02107500. And on the B/C/S if we could zoom in on that top half there, that's that top article. This is an article sir from the newspaper Glas Srpski from the 15th of February 1993. And you testified yesterday about going to New York in January -- January or February of 1993. And this article is about statements that were made by your delegation before departing for those talks. It says in the first paragraph that a delegation of the Republic of Serbian Krajina is as -- known due to depart on Tuesday and then the members of the delegation are listed, as you testified yesterday, and it included you. And I'd like to look at the second page of the English, please. And it's the last -- it's to the right on the B/C/S. There. And it says, "Furthermore, as you are aware, we have recently refuted Mr. Owen's statement that we are going to those talks for reasons of the establishment of some sort of coexistence and autonomy in the Republic of Croatia. That is not why we are going there and precisely those two words, coexistence and autonomy, will be permanently banned during the negotiations." Was that statement made by your delegation and did you endorse it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't make this statement. It was made by Boro Martinovic, as it reads here. He was the adviser to the RSK government or rather the adviser to Prime Minister Rajko Zecevic. I repeat, I'm not shrinking from your question: We had to have our maximum demands put on the table at these negotiations and that's what the papers state, and I have nothing more to add.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So this statement represented the views of the delegation which included you; is that correct? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I've given you my answer a moment ago. We had to put forth our maximum demands also to the press and those were the demands that we advocated and promoted when we sat down at the table in New York.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So when you testified yesterday that the government did not reject a single proposal made by international mediators, that was not true, was it? Right here we see a document where your delegation is rejecting a proposal made by the international mediators.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You've completely misunderstood me and I'll explain why. We accepted all proposals for negotiations but not the nuances and different opinions put forth by UNPROFOR representatives.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What about proposals put forward by Mr. Owen? You rejected those, didn't you? As it says right here in the article.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Whiting, I said that we didn't agree with the positions of UNPROFOR representatives or any other UN representatives. We, however, agreed to all proposals for negotiations, as I said yesterday. Probably we did not always endorse Mr. Owen's view points.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, could this document be admitted into evidence and given a number, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is Exhibit number 863, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, I want to -- we'll come back later the subject of negotiations and the various negotiations you participated in but I want to turn now to the situation that you found when you arrived to the RSK as foreign minister in October of 1992. You testified that in one of your first meetings with Mr. Martic, he told Cyrus Vance that the reason that the police kept long barrelled weapons in the RSK was because of attacks by the Croats. Do you remember that testimony yesterday? It's at pages 35 to 36 of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did Mr. Martic tell you that he had already made this argument to force UNPROFOR force commander General Satish Nambiar back in July of 1992 and that General Nambiar had emphatically rejected Mr. Martic's argument? Did he tell you that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know anything about that. I wasn't informed about the talks between the general and Mr. Martic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, let's look at a document and see if it refreshes your recollection. If we could see Exhibit 574 in evidence, please. I think we have to reverse the -- you have the B/C/S on the English channel and you have to reverse it for the witness. Sir, this is a memorandum, it's in evidence in our case, from General Nambiar and it's recounting a meeting held with Milan Martic on the 29th of July 1992 and if we could just scroll down to paragraph 2, I'm not going to read through the whole paragraph but essentially, in paragraph 2, in sections A and B, if we could just sort of scroll down so that the witness can see A and B, General Nambiar recounts that Mr. Martic justifies maintaining a militia of some numbers, and in section B, of maintaining long weapons for the militia for the reason that you gave, to protect themselves from Croats. And in paragraph 3, if we could look at paragraph 3, we see the response of General Nambiar. He says, "In response, I explained that we were insisting on implementing aspects pertaining to demilitarisation and carrying of side arms by police forces only with the aim of maintaining the peace and restoring normalcy to the areas as soon as possible. I reiterated that I did not see any possibility of the Security Council approving any changes to the provisions of the Vance Plan. With regard to the points raised by him, insisted he must review his stance and must provide assistance to UNPROFOR operations by issuing orders for immediate disarming and disbanding of the border militia, Milicija, and special purpose Milicija and by ensuring that all arms other than side arms worn by the regular Milicija be handed over to UNPROFOR control." Now that you've seen this document, does that -- do you recall now whether you heard, when you arrived at foreign minister in October of 1992, Mr. Martic tell you that he had already given this argument to UNPROFOR and that it had been rejected?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, is this functioning? Mr. Whiting, the contents of this meeting are identical to the meeting with Mr. Vance. You can see the extent to which there was no understanding and consideration for the situation which the Serb population found themselves in, in the RSK. Had the UN forces done something at least to protect the Serb population from the Croatian forces, I believe most of these weapons would have been handed over. The Vance Plan in its form was -- could not be implemented simply because of the actions by the Croatian forces and the automatic weapons were only a fraction of the problem and only one more thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm no I'm just going to ask you one more question before woe take a break, if I may. Would you accept that Mr. Martic had been told in July that his position was incorrect and would not be accepted and that in November of 1992, he was -- he had not done anything to abide by the Vance Plan and that he was maintaining his position that had been rejected? Would you accept that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I accept that. He was right because nobody protected the Serb population, the one provision which had been guaranteed under the Vance Plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, you've answered the question. Thank you and I'm going to ask that we take a break now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting I would like to hear your original question whether on his arrival in the cabinet, Mr. Martic had told him whether it had been said before and rejected. He has not answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'll ask him again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We will take a break now and resume at 12.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Jarcevic, when you arrived and became foreign Minister of the RSK in October of 1992, do you recall if Mr. Martic told you that he had already made the argument to the commander of UNPROFOR about the keeping of the long-barrel weapons and that this argument had been rejected?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting, I knew about the problem. It was a provision of the Vance Owen plan. That is true. And because of the Croatian aggression, unluckily it could not have been put through.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, you have not answered my question. My question is when you arrived and became the foreign minister of the RSK in 1992 you told us that you had this meeting with Mr. Martic and he made this argument to Cyrus Vance about why the Serb forces in the RSK had to keep the long barrel weapons in contravention of the Vance Plan and please listen to the question and answer the question and my question is at that time did Mr. Martic tell you that he had already made this argument to the force commander of UNPROFOR in July of 1992 and that the argument had been rejected?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I said that Mr. Martic did not inform me about his talk with Satish Nambiar. I said that before the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So in fact you were not fully informed about events that had occurred before your arrival. Is that now clear to you? Would you accept that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting, of course I didn't know each and every detail about the events up until my arrival, and I probably didn't know about all events that took place while I was minister either. That's quite normal. It's human nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, going back to the topic of the Vance Plan and demilitarisation, isn't it true that from the very start of the implementation of the Vance Plan in 1992, the Serb forces in the RSK refused to comply with the requirement of demilitarisation? Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serb forces accepted demilitarisation, and we said that they placed their heavy weaponry under two keys. That was the most important point of the demilitarisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: It's true, however, that they did not completely comply with the requirement of demilitarisation, isn't that true? They didn't from the very start and they never did; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you want to hear from me. Demilitarisation in the sense of placing heavy weaponry in that state was complied with. The Vance Plan did not provide for the army of Republic of Srpska Krajina, nor did it provide for the Croatian aggression in United Nations protected areas so both events were conditioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serb people had to defend themselves because they had no other protector and defender. What else do you want me to say? And even today, people don't have an understanding for the suffering of the Serb people.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, again, please focus on my question and just answer my question. The -- would you agree that demilitarisation required the surrendering of all weapons except for side arms?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And that was never complied with in the RSK; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right because peace was never established.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And it's also the case, sir, isn't it that the demilitarisation contemplated all forces being removed except for police and that was never really complied with either, isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I can say is the following. The units of the army of Republika Srpska Krajina existed but they did not have heavy weaponry at their disposal. And I don't know how the people would have defended themselves against the Croatian aggression had it not had the army. The United Nations offered no other solution although they promised to do so by the Vance Plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, let's --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you not feel that --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Let's look at, if we may, let's look together at a document. It's 00242533. What this is, is -- it's a report of the Secretary-General dated the 28th of September 1992, concerning the events in Croatia that -- what was happening at the time in Croatia. And since this report was issued just a month before you started, I assume that it's something that you're familiar with. It's actually Exhibit 75 in evidence. I'm sorry I didn't tell you that before. I think -- again, I think we may have to reverse the pages, reverse the -- there is -- there -- it appears that we don't have a translation of this document. So I'll just have to read you -- sir, are you all right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do I look that ill? Yes. I feel fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm sorry, it was just that you were breathing heavily and I thought --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If I may come in, yes, you did sound and looked unwell and --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But thank you for your concern.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You did look and sound unwell, and if you are not well, we must take that into account and give you time to recuperate. So you may have taken it lightly but it is asked in seriousness. Are you okay?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I feel all right. I am a little upset but only because it is difficult for me to know that the world still does not understand the seriousness of the situation that happened. But never mind, I'll survive. I'll live through it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But are you in a position to carry on with this examination or would you rather take a short break?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I don't need a break. Thank you. I can continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Okay. Thank you, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Just to follow on, if at any time you do feel any difficulty continuing, please let us know. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes I will do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, if we could look at the second page of this document, again it's Exhibit 75 in evidence and I'm interested in paragraph 4, and, sir, I'll just read -- first of all, do you recall -- I mean I know we don't have a version in your language but do you recall seeing this report when you arrived as a foreign Minister of the RSK, that this report that had been issued one month before by the United Nations? Do you recall this report?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting, please believe me, I have to give you an explanation with your indulgence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If you could just, please, answer the question, do you --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And it is linked to --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: No, please if you could just answer the question and just tell me do you recall whether or not you saw -- this report was made available to you when you became the foreign minister of the RSK? It's a yes-or-no question.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. Let's look at paragraph 4. And in paragraph 4, it reads, it talks about the first two phases of demilitarisation proceeding well but then it says, "However, the complete demilitarisation of the United Nations protected areas has been delayed by a violation of the United Nations plan which was referred to in my report of 27 July. This is the creation of new Serb militia forces designated variously as special police, border police, or multi-police brigades made up of former members of the JNA the Territorial Defence forces and irregular elements which may total as many as 16.000 armed men equipped with armoured personnel carriers, mortars and machine-guns." Now, first of all, that's true, isn't it, Mr. Jarcevic, those?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's all. All the armies were created in all the former republics of Yugoslavia including Bosnia-Herzegovina. All of them had previously been soldiers and officers of the JNA, mostly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And maintaining this force with those weapons in the RSK was a violation from the very start of the Vance Plan, isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Vance's plan was violated from all sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Let's look, please, at paragraph 34. It's on page 11 of this document. I'll just read the beginning of this paragraph and I'll ask you the same question, if this is true or not. Paragraph 34 says, "The root cause of the deterioration in the United Nations protected areas since late July has been the Knin authority's decision to create new paramilitary forces. This action is inconsistent with the demilitarisation of the United Nations protected areas and is thus a blatant violation of the United Nations plan. The damage causes all the greater because of the lawless and cruel behaviour of these so-called police units. In spite of UNPROFOR's vigilance, they have revived some of the worst features of Serb behaviour during the war in Croatia, including 'ethnic cleansing' and have created conditions of near anarchy, especially in Sector East." That's true, isn't it, sir? That's the situation that existed when you became foreign Minister of the RSK in October of 1992?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting, it is true that that is what it says in the document. However, the situation in Krajina was not portrayed as it actually was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, it's true, wasn't it, that the paramilitary forces that are described here was in blatant violation of the UN plan? I think you've already accepted that. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it isn't true that they were paramilitary formations. If the same document does not say that as referring to the Croatian forces. They were paramilitary forces as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, let's not get stuck on the word paramilitary forces. It's true, isn't it, that the forces that were created by the Knin authorities were in violation of the United Nations plan? I think you've already accepted that, isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me put it this way. I can't agree with that, that that was how the Vance Plan was violated because the Vance Plan did not regulate how the army would be deployed in Croatia and in the Republic of Srpska Krajina, how it would be used. The only thing that was said was that the forces must be de-armed in Republika Srpska Krajina which the government did, and it placed heavy weaponry under the double lock system.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm not going to go back over that, the disarming but let's move on because I think you've already given answers to those questions. Let's go on to the second part of this paragraph. It's true, isn't it, that the police units in the RSK acted in a lawless and cruel manner, as is stated in this report? Isn't that true, sir?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not true that they behaved in a cruel manner. And that they conducted ethnic cleansing. I can't agree with that because the government of the RSK did not have any such plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: We'll come back to that point. In paragraph 35 it states, "It is particularly distressing that the deteriorating security situation that is made it impossible nor UNPROFOR and UNHCR to start major programmes for the return of refugees and displaced persons to their homes." Now, it's true, isn't it, sir, that the refusal of the RSK authorities to comply with the demilitarisation made it impossible for refugees to be brought back into the RSK? Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it isn't correct because the main problem isn't mentioned, the return of the Serbs that had been expelled in far greater numbers. So that is where this document is lacking and it shows quite clearly their attitude towards the Serbs and how -- what their attitude was to the Croats, I mean the UN organs. Why was Serb expulsion not registered?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Would you agree, sir, that the Knin authorities never created the conditions in the RSK for allowing refugees to return to the RSK? Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because of the sanctions and because of a lack of reciprocity.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I want to look at another report, please, and this is one that came out while you were the foreign Minister of the RSK. It's 00241473. It's dated the 24th of November 1992. I'd like to look, please, at paragraph 11. It's on page 3 of the English. I'm not sure of the B/C/S which page it's on.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm just looking at this portion here.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm going to ask -- I'm going to ask you to focus on paragraph 11. This -- if we could on the English turn to page 3, please, thank you. In paragraph 11, it states, and this is -- follows on from the previous report which we were looking at, "complete demilitarisation of the UNPAs in accordance with the plan has been obstructed by the so-called government of the Republic of Serbian Krajina." And then it goes on to explain how these authorities have replaced the JNA and the TDF with Serb militia forces under various guises. That's true, isn't it, according to your information, what happened, JNA forces and Territorial Defence forces simply became Serb Milicija forces?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said three questions previously, in answer to them, that that's how the Croatian and the Slovenian and all the armies were created that way, from the officers and soldiers of the JNA but if you will allow me, it says here the government of the Republic of Srpska Krajina in Knin authorities in inverted commas, which means that the Security Council does not recognise us as the government. All it did was to recognise it when the Vance-Owen plan had to be signed. So you see this dual behaviour, hypocritical behaviour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, sir, sir, sir?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were worth something for one stage and not for the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, it's no -- you're not just learning for the first time today, are you, that the Republic of Serbian Krajina was never recognised as a separate country by any -- by any country in the world or by the United Nations? You have known that.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the UN Charter, there are states which are not recognised. You know that as well as I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, you didn't answer my question. You started talking about Croatia and Slovenia. My question -- my question was about the RSK. Isn't it true that JNA and Territorial Defence forces were simply renamed, and in some cases given new uniforms, as Milicija forces and retained within the RSK? Isn't that in fact what happened, as is stated here in the document?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that is quite natural because the people were born in those regions and they stayed at home on their thresholds.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, if we could look at paragraph 12, and it's evident on the screen -- maybe we could blow it up a little bit on the English. It's at the end of paragraph 12 so I think it's probably on the next page of the B/C/S. And if maybe if we could just blow up a little bit on the paragraph 12 on the English version also just make it a little easier to read. Oh, you can't. Oh, okay. We'll just have to strain our eyes. In paragraph 12 it states, it says, "For their part my representatives have insisted that the Security Council continue to hold the Belgrade authorities responsible for the implementation of the peacekeeping plan to which they had earlier agreed. It seems evident that the Belgrade authorities could, if they so chose, take measures which would have a strongly persuasive effect upon the Serb local authorities, especially in view of the considerable economic dependence of much of the UNPAs upon the FRY." That's true, isn't it, that Belgrade could have influenced the RSK on these issues at that time? You would agree with that, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not entirely. I want to say that they were relations between two states. The closest that could be imagined.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Which two states, sorry?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Republic of Srpska Krajina was a state and its statehood dates from 1630. And you're not allowing me to say that. Those state functions are far older than in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Would you now answer my question? Which two states?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and the Republic of Srpska Krajina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, sir, let's take your own -- your own situation as an example. You were made foreign Minister of the RSK but you had no ties, previous ties to the RSK, you had been recommended for the position by Serbs in Bosnia, you were paid by Belgrade, and you had your office in Belgrade. That's a little --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: -- different from two separate states, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. And I explained all that yesterday. Now you want to divide up the Serb people according to provinces or whatever you like to call them. Serb lands for me are in the Republic of Serb Krajina, in Serbia and in Bosnia. They are all Serb lands. And in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and in the old Yugoslavia, that was an area inhabited by the Serb people.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. But you don't disagree with what I stated earlier, that in fact, because of these close ties, whatever the nature was, Belgrade could have exerted considerable influence on the Serb local authorities at this time, in 1992; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We listened to their opinion, to the opinions of our ally and they were normal relations between two states.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I think you've told us that, haven't you, that it's even closer than two states, it's more like one state?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know, the measures taken by the United Nations against both drew us closer together than ever before, than was natural.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, could this document be admitted into evidence, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, the document will become Exhibit 864.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'd like now to look at a report again from the United Nations, and this one is more about human rights in the territory of the former Yugoslavia. It's 02191193. And it's dated the 17th of November 1992. Now, in your testimony earlier today, it's, I believe, at page 21 of today's transcript, you claimed that the -- any criminal activity or any discrimination against Croats within the RSK was not organised by the government. You remember that testimony?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: But that's not true, is it? Let's look at paragraph 78 of this document. It's at page 25. It states, in paragraph 78, in Sector South, which is part of the RSK, part of the so-called Republic of Krajina, local authorities practised discrimination. Courts are still not functioning properly and the investigative processes of the local police have, in the opinion of UNPROFOR officials, almost ceased to exist. This is of course -- this is of great concern to United Nations staff who collect evidence of murders, robberies, looting and other forms of criminal violence often related to ethnic cleansing. Where in accordance with their mandate such evidence is transferred to the local authorities, the latter are reluctant to take action, if not overtly uncooperative. Then in paragraph 79 it states that many people are desperate to flee the area yet before being granted permission from local authorities, these persons are often forced to sign a statement that their departure is voluntary, thus confusing the legal status of their property as well as erasing evidence of ethnic cleansing. That's true, isn't it? That's the situation in the RSK in November of 1992, when you were the foreign Minister of the RSK?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting, I will take the liberty of saying that I do not trust every one of the reports submitted to the Security Council in the form of these documents. I will give you an example in 1992 when I became minister, Nambiar spoke at the press conference in Belgrade about some chickens that were stolen in one part of Krajina without mentioning the killing of Serbs by Croats. They were killed in the fields where they were doing farm work. Now, why are no such cases recorded in any of these documents? And some of these cases were worse than the ones mentioned here. As far as the south is concerned, there is evidence to that effect and in time it will be shown to you, that those who took certain measures against Croats were arrested and punished. It says here, well, they were slow to act, but in under such circumstances where this was shortage of all the supplies, no electricity, how were these agencies supposed to operate properly?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, at the end of your answer it sounded like you were agreeing that in fact the authorities were not act -- operating properly and they were not responding to these problems so you agree that this was occurring, as it says in the document; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that they were arrested, sir. That was my answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: No but after that you say, it says they were they were slow to act but in such circumstances, where there was a shortage of all the supplies, no electricity, how were these agencies supposed to operate properly, that sounds like your trying to justify the failure of the RSK authorities to respond to and deal with what was happening in the RSK, in terms of ethnic cleansing. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that arrests were made. What more do you want of me? Now, there was this sentence here that reads, "they were slow to act." Well do you know what the Croatian authorities did not lodge a single report or no charges were brought against those who were responsible for the killings in see shack and can you imagine any slower administration of justice than that? 600 persons killed in Sisak.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, when I ask questions about what was happening in the RSK, I'm looking for answers about what was happening in the RSK. So please do not continually try to tell me what was happening in Croatia. Do you understand? We are focusing on the RSK. Now, would you agree that -- would you agree with what is stated in this document about the local authorities not dealing with the problems that were occurring in the RSK, in Sector South? Because you seem to justify it.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only remarked that documents such as this one ought to also contain evidence of ethnic cleansing against Serbs and there is only one such UN document. I was commenting on the document itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That one document, UN document, is one that you cited yesterday. It's from 1993 and we'll be looking at it later. And that document makes a reference to Serbs that are pushed out of Croatia and made refugees. And you referred to that yesterday and relied upon it. Is it the case, sir, that you credit UN documents when they support the Serbs but you dismiss it when they criticise the Serbs? Is that your stance?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not my stance. Not when you formulate it that way. But when you have 100 documents shedding negative light on the Serbs and only one shedding positive light on them, well, that is the balance that cannot be accepted because it does not correspond to the events.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, let's focus a little more carefully on paragraph 79 because this cannot be explained by shortages or lack of electricity. It says that the local authorities forced people who were leaving to sign a statement saying that it was voluntary. Thus erasing evidence of ethnic cleansing, that's true, isn't it? That occurred in Sector South at this time?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Believe me, this is the first time I hear of this case. If you want I will explain. The United Nations did not deliver their documents to the RSK government. It was by pure chance that we obtained them. If someone from UNPROFOR decided to give them these documents or if someone from the Foreign Ministry of Serbia decided to give them or Yugoslavia decided to give them to us but that was rarely or sometimes we would have some of our colleagues in New York who would ship these documents to us. That's why we who were members of the government did not have a full picture of how our government was reflected in the eyes of the other side. That was why we were immediately written off as soon as we had signed the Vance Plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: But sir, I'm sorry because yesterday, you told us you explained to us why you had your office in Belgrade and the reason, as I understood it, was that you could have contact with all the foreign governments in Belgrade and so forth. So are you now telling us that you were cut off and you did not have access to such things?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting, we would have been even more cut off had we been in Knin. I will tell you that for a period of time, the American embassy returned sealed documents to us, telling us and informing us that they had not even opened the documents to begin with. Now, that's not the proper way of proceeding in diplomatic circles.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Jarcevic, speaking about the expulsion of Croats from the RSK, you actually believe, don't you, that the expulsion of Croat civilians from the territory of the RSK was something that was engineered by the Croats so that they could blame the Serbs? Isn't that something that you believe?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do believe that most of the Croats left the RSK pursuant to a scenario by the Croatian government.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you want to explain that a little bit for us, please? What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's quite simple. This was an information war that the RSK was unable to launch on an equal footing with Croatia because Croatia had financial means to do that, they were able to pay even the international news agencies to launch the information about the mistreatment of the Croatian population although I do not wish to deny that locally speaking there were conflicts between members of Croat and Serb peoples, but always they started always by Croats killing Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to interrupt you because you're talking about something else, I think. You're talking about the information war and about propaganda and media. My question is -- you said that I do believe that most of the Croats left the RSK pursuant to a scenario by the Croatian government. And you have said elsewhere, haven't you, that in other testimony, that you believe that the expulsion of the Croat civilians from the territory of the RSK was engineered by the Croats, that they caused it, that they did it, they engineered it, and then so that they could blame the Serbs. You believe that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, because the Croatian government planned to expel Croats from the entire territory of Croatia. There are documents to that effect, even the United Nations document of the 15th of May 1993, now --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm sorry, sir?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why would Croatian government treat Serbs in Dubrovnik in a different way?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. So you believe that because -- you believe, number 1, that the Croatian government was expelling Croats from Croatia and secondly, that this is -- this causes you to believe that it was the Croatian government that caused the expulsion of Croats from the RSK? Is that -- is that what you believe, sir?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do believe that a large number of Croats left Krajina pursuant to a scenario authored by Croatia. I believe I said that a couple of times and I've made myself quite clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What is the scenario? When you say pursuant to a scenario we are sitting here not knowing what you are talking about. Can you please let us into the secret of this scenario? Can you explain this scenario?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, Mr. President, and I'm thankful for the fact that you are prepared to listen to my explanation. You see, in 1990 and 1991 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm listening to everything that is being said here.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1990 and 1991, the Croatian parliament amended the constitution whereby practically placing Serbs outside law, not only those outside of the Republic of Krajina but -- or rather, in Krajina but all of them. They amended the part of the constitution which stated that strategic decisions could not be taken without full consent of members of both ethnic groups. Only Croat MPs voted in -- for that amendment. Is that not -- does that not constitute placing Serbs outside law? What followed was the fleeing of Serbs from Croatia. You can find that in the bulletin issued by the Croatian government this year, where it is clearly shown that at one of its meetings, the government decision says that Serbs are being killed by members of the army, police and civilians. This particular scenario was workable in the large towns but not in the Krajina where there was the majority Serb population, who got organised and tried to thwart this -- these intentions by the Croatian government. Now, you have 400.000 people who were expelled from the area. What could the people who hid themselves and tried to get organised, what could they expect to become of them? They had enjoyed their statehood ever since 1630. That was the full picture. Now, of course, the only solution Croatia was left with at that point was to place the blame on the other side as well but this was already at the time when Croatia had expelled 400.000 Serbs. They organised the departure of Croats. Of course, I do not wish to deny that in these interethnic conflicts some of the Croats were forced to flee because they were outnumbered by Serbs. These were armed Croats who were defeated and had to withdraw with their families. This was a terrible scene but nevertheless it was organised by the Croatian government and it was to cover up for the expulsion of Serbs from Dubrovnik, Split and Zadar. Let me tell you, in Zadar, this small sea side town there were 26.000 Serbs there and 25.000 Croats. All of the 26.000 Serbs were expelled from there and arrived in the territory of the RSK. Do you think you were able to persuade anyone of them not to take up arms and defend themselves? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I hear what you say. You're talking mainly about the expulsion of Serbs by Croats. I'm not quite clear how all this fits into a creation by the government of Croatia which engineers the expulsion of Croats.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The government organised the evacuation of Croats from the territory of the RSK in order to accuse the authorities of the RSK and the JNA of having expelled these people. Many of them left the area in an organised fashion just as the terrorist organisation in Kosovo-Metohija was to do later on with the evacuation of the Albanian population from the area in 1999.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I just ask you, when you say the government organised the evacuation of Croats from the territory of the RSK, in order to accuse the authorities of the RSK, what specific actions did the government take in the organisation of that evacuation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When the Croatian parliament amended the constitution, the Croatian government started setting up Croatian police station in Serb-inhabited areas, dismissing Serb members of the police and hiring Croat ones. The same scenario was applied in 1941, when Croat police officers were calling out 100 or 200 people, Serb people, and killing them. Serbs were afraid of the fact that this might all happen again. Locally the government was able to organise the evacuation of Croats and to make it seem an expulsion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What do you mean locally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The local authorities, Your Honour, because if you dismiss a Serb police officer and you hire a Croat police officer instead, of course this person will be receiving instructions from his minister and his government. And he would be receiving instructions the same way the police officer in Dubrovnik received them when he expelled 2.200 Serbs from the area. Why should a Croat police officer in Krajina behave any differently?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: My question to you is: How does the firing of a Serb policeman and replacing him with a Croat cause the movement of Croats out of a particular area? I would imagine it would actually attract the Croats to the area.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, those police stations were the ones who started perpetrating crimes against Serbs. Serbs in turn organised themselves and put up resistance. If a Croat police officer was killed anywhere, it was only the result of him having killed or of the fact that the Serb civilians had previously been killed. This was something that the Croatian government made use of for its own purposes to evacuate the Croat population from Krajina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I think I understand you, just to make clear that I understand you correctly I'm going to tell you my understanding and I want you to tell me if I'm right. What you are saying is that because of all these things that you say the Croat government did, dismissing Serb police and employing Croat police, the Serbs had to defend themselves, and in defending themselves drove the Croats out and the Croatian government blamed the Serbs for driving the Croatians out. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, you have to understand the extent of the confusion that prevailed there but I'll give you an example. Ten Serbs were dismissed from a company.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm asking you a simple question. Am I understanding you correctly when I say what I've just said? You can just say no, you don't understand me correctly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you've understood that the Croatian government by applying its measures brought about interethnic conflicts and organised the departure of Croats from the Republic of Serbian Krajina, then your understanding is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's not what you said. You said the Serbs took arms in defence of themselves and that's why the Croats left. Now you saying the Croat government organised the departure of Croats from RSK. I'm not quite sure. Those are two different statements now, different positions. Unless by organise, you mean the whole action of dismissing --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Killing of Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... and playing Croat so as to provoke a revenge or a self defence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that the Croatian government organised the dismissal of Serbs, that it set up police stations in Serb settlements, that it was the Croat police officers who perpetrated the first killings of Serbs, and that then, in turn, Serbs organised themselves to defends themselves from actions of the Croat police, that then an interethnic conflict broke out, the JNA got involved, and the Croatian government used the entire situation to its own benefit to have the Croatian population evacuated from the Republic of the Serbian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. I think I can't take it much further than that. It's fine. Thank you very much, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm going to try to take it a bit fur. As I understand what you're saying is that -- tell me if I'm correct, that the Croatian government actually intentionally organised the evacuation or the expulsion of the Croat population from the RSK so that they could blame the Serbs. Isn't that really what you're saying? That's what you believe?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I said and if I said so, that means that I believe what I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, we talked earlier a little bit about media and about propaganda and I want to look, please, at paragraph 95 of this document. It's on page 28. And in this paragraph of this UN document, it states that the information blockade which has existed since the beginning of hostilities in the former Yugoslavia has far-reaching consequences. The government controlled electronic media and press have engaged in a one-sided and nationalistic propaganda campaign. The official media have done nothing to distance themselves from the politics of intolerance and as a result have fed the fires of hatred. That's true, isn't it, Mr. Jarcevic, about what was happening in 1992?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just tell me, Mr. Prosecutor, whether article 95 has to do with the mass media in the Republic of Serbian Krajina because that's not what it says here. Further down in the text, there is mention of JuTel and that was not a Krajina broadcasting company but that of Yugoslavia, and it was run by people who were of Yugoslav orientation, not of pro-Serbian orientation. That's why it's called Yugoslav television, JuTel.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: To answer your question, it's -- this section in the report is about Serbia, and the media that's being referenced here is the Serbian media. Now, if you could answer my question, is this an accurate description of the official media that was coming out of Serbia at the time?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, the sentence reads further on that this concerns both the Croat and Serbian media. Therefore it relates to both.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: It does, you're right. My question is about the Serbian media. Do you want -- can you answer my question about the Serbian media? Is it accurate in what it says about the Serbian media?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not accurate if they are equalised with the Croatian ones. They were just a pale image of the hatred displayed in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Forget about Croatia for a moment, sir. Just answer my question about the Serbian media. Is it true that the government-controlled electronic media and press have engaged in a one-sided and nationalistic propaganda campaign and have fed the fires of hatred? Is that true about the media that was coming out of Serbia, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Let's look at the conclusions and recommendations of this report. It's at paragraph 134.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What page?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: It's on page 38, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: In paragraphs 134 and 135, talk about how ethnic cleansing has continued and intensified in both Bosnia and Herzegovina and also in Croatia. In paragraph 135 it states, the continuation of ethnic cleansing is a deliberate effort to create a fait accompli in flagrant disregard of international commitments entered into by those who carry out and benefit from ethnic cleansing. In paragraph 136, it states, "The Serbian authorities in de facto control of certain territories in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and in the United Nations protected --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In view of the fact that Mr. Jarcevic testified to the situation in Yugoslavia in the examination-in-chief, the Defence did not want to raise an objection about the fact that the Prosecutor keeps examining the witness on a topic that was not the subject of the examination-in-chief. Therefore, he did not testify to the situation in Yugoslavia. The Prosecutor keeps insisting on the topic of the media war in a way which goes far beyond the scope of the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I just want to read what you said because I didn't understand you. I don't understand what you're saying, Mr. Milovancevic. You seem to contradict yourself. In the first sentence you say in view of the fact that Mr. Jarcevic testified to the situation in Yugoslavia in the examination-in-chief. Testified. And then you say, therefore he did not testify to the situation in Yugoslavia later. Those two sentences are contradictory. So now, I do not understand what you mean because -- let me just finish -- let me just finish. There is a whole -- according to the counts, the charges against the accused, there is also the whole question of the JCE. And the JCE would mean, as I understand it, collaboration between the people in the rest of Yugoslavia and the people in the RSK, unless I misunderstand that. So I'm not quite sure what you mean, this is not relevant to the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. That's not what I said at all. I said something quite different and it is this: That the cross-examination by the Prosecutor must be linked to the examination-in-chief conducted by the Defence. The Prosecutor could have brought in its own witness to testify about the media war. But Mr. Jarcevic wasn't examined on that topic at all. And now the Prosecutor has raised the issue -- an issue that this witness isn't a witness -- hasn't testified about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I think -- let Mr. Whiting respond rather than me answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, first of all I think it would be artificial to separate out the media war as a separate topic. It's really of a piece, as is clear in this document, and should be clear in the questions and answers, it is part of the campaign of ethnic cleansing that this witness has testified about in direct examination and it's fair to ask these questions in cross-examination. Secondly, the rules of the Tribunal require the parties to put their case to the witness and if the witness has -- is in a position to provide information that would advance the case of either party, we are required under the rules to put those questions to the witness so I think these questions are within bounds and certainly fair.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, do you have any reply to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the answer is short. I did not say that the questions weren't relevant. They are linked to the indictment and a series of counts in the indictment but all I'm trying to do is to say that the cross-examination must follow the examination-in-chief and the topic that the witness testified about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But you're not replying to the response by the Prosecution by what you're saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is our response, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Objection overruled.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, when we were interrupted I was reading some paragraphs, some parts of paragraphs 134, 135 and I had just gotten to 136, and I don't recall if I had read it or not, but it states that "the Serbian authorities in de facto control of certain territories in Bosnia and Herzegovina and in the United Nations protected areas bear primary responsibility for the policy of ethnic cleansing carried out there. The command of the Yugoslav National Army and the political leadership of the Republic of Serbia also share responsibility for this policy which could not have been continued until the present time without their active support. This contradicts what you testified to in direct examination, sir, doesn't it, that the authorities of -- in the RSK were not involved in -- or did not bear any -- did not bear any responsibility for the ethnic cleansing that occurred in the RSK?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting, I still state that the government of the Republic of Srpska Krajina and assembly never organised any ethnic cleansing, ethnic cleansing of Croats in the Republic of RSK. And if I might be allowed to say we discussed this with the co-presidents as well during these -- the drafting of these and similar documents and I asked Mr. Owen why there was no control over the Croatian authorities because it conducted the greatest ethnic cleansing and his answer was, and Vance's before that, we have no resolution which would make it incumbent upon us to do so. And so with that example you can see how faulty these documents are of the UN Security Council, because there are no obligations to control the Croatian authorities I which means you can put the Serbs outside the law, you can expel the Serbs and nobody will ever be held responsible for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: But let me put the question to you again. Are you saying that what's contained in these paragraphs 134, 135 and 136, that I read to you, are you saying that that's not true? But aside whether it should have also said something about Croatia. Put that aside. Put that objection aside. Focus please on these paragraphs. These paragraphs are true, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are not true because the government did not organise ethnic cleansing, nor did it incite it in any way.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, could this document be admitted into evidence, please, and given a number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, this document will become Exhibit 865.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The document is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Earlier today, sir, you were asked some questions about Skabrnja. It's at page 22 of the transcript. And you said as you're asking me about Skabrnja, that was the Yugoslav People's Army over there and in my opinion those crimes should not be linked to responsibility and accountability of people from the Republic of Srpska Krajina, although Yugoslav officers are not to blame as much for those crimes as are the Croatian officers and soldiers. So you agree, don't you, then, that there were crimes committed by Serb forces in Skabrnja in the conflict in 1991, in November of 1991? You agree with that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't give you a direct answer to your question, sir. I just said that at the time the Yugoslav People's Army had officers and soldiers belonging to all the nations and nationalities of Yugoslavia, percentage wise there were as many Serbs as there were in terms of the population.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: In your answer, in your answer, you referred to crimes -- the crimes in Skabrnja and who should be held responsible for them. Aren't you accepting then that there were crimes in Skabrnja? That's the first question. Yes or no. Do you accept that there were crimes in Skabrnja?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is so well known, there were crimes on both sides, at the same period.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, my next question is are you aware, did you learn, that in the attack on Skabrnja, it was not just the forces of the Yugoslav People's Army that participated but also the forces of the police and the Territorial Defence? Are you aware of that, sir?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm aware of the following: The Croats perpetrated some crime over there and then there was reaction on the part of the Yugoslav People's Army and the Serbs from the area. I don't know the details of the case and please believe me when I say that because I was outside the RSK at the time and did not study these documents in detail, the documents linked to Skabrnja, I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And sir, you accept that in the action taken by the JNA and the police and the Territorial Defence, in November of 1991 in Skabrnja, that crimes were committed by those Serb forces? You accept that, don't you, sir?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once again I say that I can't accept the fact that the JNA was a Serb army during that period of time. Don't force me to say that. It was a Yugoslav army composed of all the nations and nationalities, all ethnic groups, and even one Albanian died wearing the uniform of the JNA. He was killed by Croatian soldiers. That is what I know. So we cannot say it was a Serb army.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You're avoiding answering my question, sir. The question is in the attack on Skabrnja by the JNA, the Territorial Defence from the area of the SAO Krajina and the police of the area of the SAO Krajina in the attack by those forces on Skabrnja in November of 1991, crimes were committed. Is that correct, sir? You know that.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I did hear of crimes being committed by the Serbs were just in the Territorial Defence and in other units of a local nature. Once again, I state that the JNA was not a Serb army.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think this would be a convenient time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Whiting. We will stand adjourned until tomorrow morning at 9.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 14th day of July, 2006, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.46 p.m.,
